anchors.extracted: Single-author review published under the heading 'Basel Proceedings', by an author from the Clinical Biology Laboratory of Ghent University Hospital, with no stated search, selection criteria or appraisal. Data on detection times come from controlled administration to volunteers, in many studies at doses the author calls relatively low compared with street doses, or from people forced to stop (often chronic) use, for example on imprisonment or detoxification, which gives no information on the detection time after a single dose. In Tables 1 to 3 (blood, urine, oral fluid) the times are based as much as possible on the methods' limits of quantification or detection rather than on cutoffs. Detection time depends on the dose, the preparation and route, acute or chronic use, the fluid analysed, the detection limit or cutoff, the molecule or metabolite sought, the pH and concentration of urine or oral fluid, and individual differences in metabolism (and, in the abstract, renal clearance).

anchors.extracted: In children and adolescents there were some head-to-head trials and the networks were well connected; in adults there were only placebo-controlled trials, so the networks were star shaped. Restricted to FDA-licensed doses, only amphetamines or lisdexamfetamine were consistently associated with higher blood pressure than placebo in adults, which the authors suggest may indicate dose dependency (numbers only in the appendix). Four trials gave 24-week results and none reported long-term results. The analyses used trial-level averages: the authors say some people may have larger changes, report more outlier values on the medicines than on placebo (numbers only in the appendix), and could not identify who is at higher risk; most trials were industry sponsored.

anchors.locator: The Drug Information and Monitoring System (DIMS), 2nd paragraph; Office testing, 1st paragraph (left column, continued in the right column) and 2nd paragraph
anchors.source_read: PDF (version of record), Drug Testing and Analysis 3, 621–634: all pages read; p. 622 rendered at 100 dpi
anchors.extracted: Most testing facilities can identify some tablets the moment they are handed in ('office testing'): staff register diameter, thickness, weight, colour, groove, light or dark speckling and logo (and its design), do a Marquis reagent test, and look the tablet up in an online database, updated weekly, of tablets recently analysed in a laboratory. Because ecstasy tablets are usually made in large batches, a match is 'recognized': its average MDMA content and variation are taken as known (neither is reported) and it need not go to the laboratory. Results of recognized tablets that people still have analysed are used for validation, said to have shown 99% reliability (no data). On average 30% of tablets are determined this way; tablets not recognized, or in doubt, are sent to the laboratory.

anchors.extracted: For each tablet the services recorded logo, diameter, thickness, weight, colour and groove; if a tablet from a batch had already been analysed by GC–MS at least three times, its colour-test result and these features were taken as sufficient identification, and the person was given the batch's average content and range.
